w: Founded in 597, rebuilt from 1070 and again after an 1174 fire, the cathedral holds the site where Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in 1170. Pilgrims flocking to his shrine forced a Gothic eastward extension; before the Reformation it was also a Benedictine priory, Christ Church.
_facts: Founded in 597; rebuilt 1070-1077 and again after the 1174 fire
Site of the 1170 murder of Archbishop Thomas Becket
Eastward extensions built to accommodate pilgrim traffic to Becket's shrine
Was the seat of the Priory of Christ Church, a Benedictine community, before the Reformation

w: Paved by the Romans over an earlier Briton trackway, this road linked the Kent ports of Dover, Richborough, Lympne and Reculver through Canterbury to London and on to Wroxeter. It later marked the Danelaw's border with Wessex and Mercia, and tradition places Boudica's final defeat somewhere along its route.
s: Roman road tradition ties to Boudica's defeat
_facts: Roman road running from Dover and London to Wroxeter, via Canterbury
Connected the Kent ports of Dover, Richborough, Lympne and Reculver to London
Later formed the Danelaw's southwestern border with Wessex and Mercia
Traditionally cited as the site of the Romans' defeat of Boudica

w: Built in 1848 for a congregation founded in 1720, this is considered the finest surviving example of an Egyptian Revival synagogue, a style shared by only a handful of buildings worldwide. Worship ended around 1911; since 1982 King's School has used it as a music recital hall.
s: A rare Egyptian Revival synagogue turned recital hall
_facts: Congregation established 1720; building completed 1848
Considered the best surviving example of Egyptian Revival synagogue architecture
Worship ceased around 1911; Grade II listed since 1973
Used by King's School as a music performance space since 1982

w: Recognised as the oldest church still in use anywhere in the English-speaking world, St Martin's forms part of the Canterbury World Heritage Site alongside the cathedral and St Augustine's Abbey. It has belonged to the joint parish of St Martin and St Paul since 1668.
s: The oldest church still in use in the English-speaking world
_facts: Oldest existing church in the English-speaking world
Oldest English church building still in ecclesiastical use
Part of the Canterbury World Heritage Site with the cathedral and St Augustine's Abbey
Part of the benefice of St Martin and St Paul Canterbury since 1668

w: This Palladian house, built in 1704 by Brook Bridges, 1st Baronet, passed down to a granddaughter who married Jane Austen's brother; Austen herself was a regular visitor to the estate. The Grade II* listed house sits within 15 acres of gardens ranked among the finest in southeast England.
s: Jane Austen's regular country retreat near Canterbury
_facts: Palladian house built 1704 by Brook Bridges, 1st Baronet

15 acres of gardens considered among the finest in southeast England

w: This Queen Anne mansion, built in 1701 for Elizabeth Aucher on the site of an older house, has been Grade I listed since 1954. Its grounds, with an 18th-century ice house and a bridge over the Nailbourne, are the subject of ongoing archaeological digs led by the University of Cambridge.
s: A 1701 mansion still being excavated by Cambridge
_facts: Queen Anne house built 1701, commissioned by Elizabeth Aucher

w: Dating probably from the 11th century, this partly Anglo-Saxon stone church is the only pre-Norman church still standing within Canterbury's former city walls. Grade I listed since 1949, it gives its name to the surrounding St Mildred's quarter of the old city centre.
s: The only pre-Norman church inside the old city walls
_facts: Partly Anglo-Saxon church, probably dating from the 11th century

w: Founded in the 7th century on the ruins of the Roman fort of Regulbium, this minster was granted to a priest named Bassa by King Ecgberht of Kent in 669; a Kentish king was later buried there. Its Saxon builders reused Roman stone and tile, and twin towers were added in the 12th century.
s: A Saxon minster built from a Roman fort's stones

w: This 11th-century church gives its name to the Canterbury district on the left bank of the Stour. Its association with the deaths of Thomas Becket and Thomas More has made it a place of pilgrimage, and the Grade I listed building was restored in 1878-80 by architect Ewan Christian.
s: A pilgrim church tied to Becket and Thomas More
